rules.plain_language_rule: Lifestyle behaviors outside formal training can materially influence recovery, adaptation, and performance.
Sleep is a central recovery behavior and should be monitored when practical.
Higher training and competition demands increase the importance of adequate recovery opportunity.
Sleep monitoring should consider both quantity and perceived quality.
Sleep data should be interpreted as trends rather than relying only on individual nights.
Sleep and wellness information provides context for performance but should not be treated as proof of causation.
Repeated inadequate sleep should generate a coaching/recovery flag rather than an automatic diagnosis.
Short sleep has been associated with increased injury occurrence in some athlete populations, but sleep duration alone should not be used to predict injury.
Sleep extension and appropriately timed naps may support athlete recovery and performance.
The platform should contain practical sleep-hygiene education.
Recovery interventions should be matched to the athlete’s identified issue rather than prescribed identically to everyone.
Post-intervention feedback should be recorded so the system can learn which recovery strategies are useful for the individual athlete.
Persistent sleep problems should trigger appropriate human follow-up and potentially professional referral, not automated medical diagnosis.
Cognitive demands outside rugby can influence training and match readiness.
Mental fatigue may impair decision-making speed, decision accuracy, technical execution, or physical performance in some contexts.
Digital activity should be considered one potential contributor to cognitive load rather than assumed to be its sole cause.
Social-media use should be interpreted alongside sleep, stress, school/work demands, and general wellbeing.
The system should monitor perceived mental fatigue rather than unnecessarily surveilling an athlete’s device use.
Persistent high mental fatigue should create a coaching flag and conversation opportunity.
Digital habits that interfere with sleep or preparation can become targets for education and behavior modification.
Mental-fatigue and psychological-wellbeing measures should remain separate variables.
Recovery interventions such as breathing, meditation, relaxation, or low-intensity movement may be offered when appropriate, with athlete feedback recorded afterward.
Youth athlete digital and wellbeing data should be handled with heightened privacy protections.
